name: Patrice Lumumba
info: Patrice Lumumba (1925–1961) was a Congolese politician and independence leader, the first prime minister of the First Congolese Republic in 1960, who was dismissed, arrested and executed by Katangan authorities within months of independence.

facts.born: 2 July 1925 as Isaïe Tasumbu Tawosa, in Onalua, Katakokombe region, Kasaï province, Belgian Congo; a Tetela, known in that group as Élias Okit'Asombo; son of Julienne Wamato Lomendja and François Tolenga Otetshima, a farmer
facts.died: 17 January 1961 near Elisabethville in Katanga, shot by firing squads; his body was dug up and later dissolved in acid
facts.role: Leader of the Congolese National Movement (MNC) from 1958 until his death; first prime minister of the First Congolese Republic, June to September 1960
facts.known: the Congolese independence movement; the MNC; his independence day speech of 30 June 1960; the Congo Crisis; his dismissal by Kasa-Vubu and arrest after Mobutu's coup; his execution in Katanga; Lumumbisme

t: Born Isaïe Tasumbu Tawosa to a Tetela family in the Kasaï, Lumumba worked as a postal clerk and beer salesman before leading the Mouvement National Congolais from 1958, a party that did not draw on a particular ethnic base.

He became prime minister in June 1960, but within days an army mutiny, a Belgian intervention and the secession of Katanga began the Congo Crisis, and President Kasa-Vubu dismissed him on 5 September.

Arrested by Mobutu's troops in December 1960 and executed in Katanga on 17 January 1961, he has been remembered above all as a martyr, a status that historians such as David Van Reybrouck say owes more to his death than to his political successes.
dyk: On 30 June 1960, Lumumba, who had not been scheduled to speak, answered King Baudouin's independence day speech with an impromptu address; Time magazine called it a "vicious attack".
ev: Born Isaïe Tasumbu Tawosa in Onalua, in the Kasaï province of the Belgian Congo
Helps found the Mouvement National Congolais and becomes its leader; attends the All-African Peoples' Conference in Accra in December
Arrested in late October for inciting an anti-colonial riot in Stanleyville in which 30 people were killed, and sentenced to six months in prison
Independence is declared on 30 June; Lumumba, prime minister since the vote of 23 and 24 June, gives his impromptu speech, and the army mutiny of July opens the Congo Crisis
Kasa-Vubu dismisses him on 5 September; Mobutu announces a coup on 14 September; Mobutu's troops arrest Lumumba at the Sankuru River on 1 December
Flown to Katanga on 17 January and shot that night; his body is later dug up and dissolved in acid
His remaining tooth is handed to his family in Brussels on 20 June, and he is buried in Kinshasa on 30 June

sections.early:
Patrice Émery Lumumba was born on 2 July 1925 as Isaïe Tasumbu Tawosa in Onalua, in the Katakokombe region of the Kasaï province of the Belgian Congo. His parents were Julienne Wamato Lomendja and François Tolenga Otetshima, a farmer. He belonged to the Tetela ethnic group, in which he was called Élias Okit'Asombo; his original surname means "heir of the cursed". He had three brothers and one half-brother. Raised in a Catholic family, he attended a Protestant primary school, a Catholic missionary school and the government post office training school, where he passed the one-year course with distinction. He spoke Tetela, French, Lingala, Swahili and Tshiluba.

He was known as a vocal, precocious young man who pointed out his teachers' errors in front of his peers. He took an interest in the Enlightenment ideals of Jean-Jacques Rousseau and Voltaire, was fond of Molière and Victor Hugo, and wrote poetry, many of his works with anti-imperialist themes. He worked as a travelling beer salesman in Léopoldville and as a postal clerk in Stanleyville for eleven years. He married three times: Henriette Maletaua in 1945 (divorced 1947), Hortense Sombosia in 1947 (divorced 1951) and, in 1951, Pauline Opangu, who was 14 years old at the time. A relationship with Pauline Kie produced a son, François Lumumba.
sections.rise:
In 1952 Lumumba was hired as personal assistant to the French sociologist Pierre Clément, who was studying Stanleyville, and he co-founded and became president of the town's chapter of an alumni association, ADAPÉS. In 1955 he became regional head of the Cercles of Stanleyville and joined the Liberal Party of Belgium. After a study tour in Belgium in 1956 he was arrested on a charge of embezzling $2500 from the post office; he was convicted and sentenced a year later to 12 months' imprisonment and a fine. He wrote his autobiography in 1956 and 1957; it was published after his death, in 1962.

After his release he helped found the Mouvement National Congolais (MNC) in 1958 and quickly became its leader. Unlike other Congolese parties of the time, the MNC did not draw on a particular ethnic base. Its platform included independence, gradual Africanisation of the government, state-led economic development and neutrality in foreign affairs. In December 1958 he represented the party at the All-African Peoples' Conference in Accra, hosted by Kwame Nkrumah. In 1959 the MNC split into the majority MNC-L, led by Lumumba, and the more radical, federalist MNC-K. In late October 1959 he was arrested for inciting an anti-colonial riot in Stanleyville in which 30 people were killed, and sentenced to six months. Pressure from delegates upset by his trial won his release to attend the Brussels round table, which on 27 January 1960 set independence for 30 June.
sections.deeds:
The MNC won a plurality in the May 1960 elections. After the Belgian minister Walter Ganshof van der Meersch ended Lumumba's attempt to form a government on 17 June and named Joseph Kasa-Vubu formateur, the other parties would not support a government without Lumumba, and the king appointed him formateur instead. On 23 and 24 June the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate approved his 37-member coalition government. His goals were to improve the quality of life of the Congolese and to unify the country as a centralised state by eliminating tribalism and regionalism.

At the independence ceremony on 30 June, King Baudouin spoke of the "genius" of Leopold II. Lumumba, not scheduled to speak, replied that independence had been won by fighting, "a fight in which we were spared neither privation nor suffering". On 5 July the Force Publique mutinied. Lumumba dismissed its commander, renamed it the Armée Nationale Congolaise and appointed Victor Lundula and Joseph Mobutu to lead it. Belgium sent 6,000 troops on 10 July; Katanga declared independence on 11 July with Belgian government and mining company support. Lumumba appealed to the United Nations, then to the Soviet premier, Nikita Khrushchev, and travelled to New York, Washington, Ottawa and several African states seeking help. In August he sent troops against the secession of South Kasai.
sections.opponents:
Western media criticised the independence speech; the Belgian government regarded him as communist, anti-white and anti-Western, and many other Western governments agreed. On 9 August 1960 he proclaimed a state of emergency, outlawed associations formed without government sanction, asserted the right to ban publications, arrested the editor of the Courrier d'Afrique and shut down the Belga and Agence France-Presse wire services. The Congolese army's campaign in South Kasai, which Lumumba ordered, devolved into ethnic violence and massacres of Luba civilians; the people and politicians of South Kasai held him personally responsible. Kasa-Vubu declared that only a federalist government could bring peace, and the Catholic Church openly criticised the government. His own chef de cabinet, Damien Kandolo, acted as a spy for the Belgian government.

Historians have judged him differently. Belgian literature portrayed him as incompetent, demagogic, aggressive and communist. Africanists such as Jean-Claude Willame saw him as an intransigent, unrealistic idealist without a tangible programme, greatly responsible for the crisis that brought him down. Jean-Paul Sartre thought his goals unattainable in 1960 but saw him as a martyr and the victim of events he could scarcely control. According to the sociologist Ludo De Witte, both views overstate his political weaknesses and isolation. Lumumba did not espouse a comprehensive political or economic platform.
sections.last:
On 5 September 1960 Kasa-Vubu announced over the radio that he had dismissed Lumumba and six ministers, citing the massacres in South Kasai and the involvement of the Soviets. Lumumba denounced the dismissal as illegitimate and declared the president deposed. The Chamber voted 60 to 19 to annul both declarations, and the Senate gave Lumumba's government a vote of confidence, 49 to zero with seven abstentions. On 14 September Mobutu announced a "peaceful revolution" that neutralised the president, the governments and Parliament until 31 December. Lumumba was confined to his residence, where a cordon of UN peacekeepers kept Mobutu's troops from arresting him.

On 27 November he left the capital for Stanleyville, where Antoine Gizenga's supporters had established a rival government. Mobutu's troops caught up with the party on 1 December at the Sankuru River; Lumumba went back across by ferry after his wife and child were captured, and was arrested. He was held at Camp Hardy in Thysville from 3 December with Maurice Mpolo and Joseph Okito. On 17 January 1961 the three were flown to Elisabethville, in Katanga, where Katangan officers beat and tortured them. That night they were shot by firing squads commanded by a Belgian officer, Julien Gat, in the presence of Moïse Tshombe and other Katangan and Belgian officials. The bodies were buried, then dug up; Lumumba's was cut up and dissolved in sulfuric acid. Katangan radio announced on 13 February that he had been killed by villagers after escaping.
sections.legacy:
A group of historians appointed by the Belgian parliament concluded in 2001 that Belgian government authorities helped oust Lumumba, opposed any reconciliation, insisted on his arrest and supported his transfer to Katanga without ruling out that he might be executed there. In 2002 Belgium formally apologised for its role, admitting "moral responsibility". In September 1960 President Eisenhower authorised a CIA plan to poison him, which was not carried out. In 2022 the Belgian prime minister, Alexander De Croo, apologised again, and Lumumba's remaining tooth was handed to his family and buried in Kinshasa.

His ideological legacy is called Lumumbisme, usually framed as nationalism, pan-Africanism, nonalignment and social progressivism. Mobutu proclaimed him a national hero in 1966. According to the political scientist Georges Nzongola-Ntalaja, his greatest legacy for the Congo is the ideal of national unity. His image remained unpopular in southern Kasai for years because of the 1960 campaign against the Baluba.

Scholars note that he became a martyr after death. David Van Reybrouck wrote that he owed this status more to the horrible end of his life than to his political successes; Pedro Monaville wrote that his global iconic status was not commensurate with his more complex legacy in the Congo. No consensus has been reached on his political legacy.

summary: Patrice Lumumba (1925–1961) led the Congolese National Movement and became the Congo's first prime minister at independence in June 1960. Dismissed in September, arrested after Mobutu's coup and shot in Katanga in January 1961, he is remembered chiefly as a martyr, though historians disagree about his political record.
references: Emmanuel Gerard, Death in the Congo: Murdering Patrice Lumumba (Harvard University Press, 2015)
Catherine Hoskyns, The Congo Since Independence: January 1960 – December 1961 (Oxford University Press, 1965)
Thomas R. Kanza, The Rise and Fall of Patrice Lumumba: Conflict in the Congo (Schenkman Books, Inc., 1994)
notes: Dates: birth 2 July 1925 and death 17 January 1961 as the lead gives them; the execution time (21:40-21:43) is attributed in the article to a later Belgian parliamentary inquiry and is left out.

The article says the 'Union of African States' agreement with Nkrumah, the CIMCO contract, the 9 August state of emergency details and the Mobutu-era banknote exist; only the state of emergency and press measures are used here.
The briefcase documents published after 14 September (some almost certainly forgeries) are left out for space.
UK involvement (Howard Smith's remark, the claim about Daphne Park, which the article says the government did not corroborate) is left out; the CIA poison plan is given as the article states it.
Pauline Opangu's age (14 in 1951) is stated as the article gives it.
The article contradicts itself slightly on South Kasai: one passage says the secession was not quashed until the following year; the text only says the army was withdrawn in September.
The article says the Sûreté and informants fed Lumumba rumours; left out. The Belgian apology is given as 2002 in the lead and the 2022 apology in the repatriation section.

The article's 'Early life' section hedges nothing about the 'Katakokombe region' spelling; used as given. The execution is described as ordered by Katangan leaders and the last stage carried out by Belgian contract officers (Frans Verscheure); here only the firing squads under Gat and the presence of Tshombe are named.
Left out: honours, popular culture, films, songs, the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations tribute, Malcolm X's quotation (a ranking), vandalism of the mausoleum in 2024.
Judgement of 'Red Africa' scholars and Patricia Goff's analysis of his narrative left out for space.
